paragraphs.heading: The most complex system in the room
paragraphs.edited: Take a look at the room around you and ask yourself a simple question. What do you think is the most complex system that stores the most information? Maybe there's a computer in the room, maybe there's a tablet, maybe you're streaming this on your cell phone. Are those the most complex systems that store vast amounts of information? The answer is clearly no. The most complex system in the room is you. To be specific, it's your DNA.

paragraphs.heading: Nine feet in a single cell
paragraphs.edited: Your body is made up of around 100 trillion cells. The DNA in one cell of your body, just one cell, if it were unwound, would be about nine feet in length. That means all the DNA in your body strung together would go from here to the sun and back about 70 times. This raises a very troubling and difficult question, both for naturalism and for pantheism: what can best explain the source of this vast amount of information? What worldview best explains the origin of DNA?

paragraphs.heading: Monkeys typing Shakespeare
paragraphs.edited: To explain the rise of information that we see in nature, some naturalists have devised a test simply called the monkeys typing Shakespeare theorem. The idea is that if you have a bunch of monkeys and enough computers and enough time, eventually one of the monkeys will sit down, through a purely blind lucky process, and type out all the works of Shakespeare. The point is to explain the rise of information in nature, and in DNA specifically, through a purely blind process.

paragraphs.heading: What chance can actually produce
paragraphs.edited: In my book Understanding Intelligent Design, my co-author William Dembski and I cited a quantum computational physicist by the name of Seth Lloyd. What Seth Lloyd did is mathematically compute exactly how much information could arise by chance, given all the resources of the universe. He concluded that chance alone could not produce all the works of Shakespeare. It couldn't produce one work of Shakespeare, not a chapter, not a page, not a paragraph. All the resources of the universe by chance at best could produce four lines from one work of Shakespeare: "To be or not to be, that is the question. Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer."

paragraphs.heading: Someone actually ran the experiment
paragraphs.edited: Some time ago some students and a professor decided to actually test the monkeys typing Shakespeare theorem. They took some monkeys and put them in a zoo with some old computers and typewriters to see if one of the monkeys would sit down and type out Romeo and Juliet or Hamlet. The first monkey picked up a rock, climbed up on the computer and tried to bash it. Some other monkeys climbed up on top and actually went to the bathroom on the computer. But before you discount this experiment: in the time that they were in there, these monkeys produced roughly six pages of written text: a string of A's, L's, M's, J's and an occasional S. Not a single word.

paragraphs.heading: A message in the sand
paragraphs.edited: In reality, whenever we come across information and can trace it back to its causal source, we always find a mind. Imagine you come visit me in Southern California and we go walking on the beach. All of a sudden we stop, because we see engraved in the sand a heart that says "Sean loves Stephanie." Stephanie is my wife. Now, I know none of you would stop and say, "That's crazy. I've heard about earthquakes in Southern California, but I had no idea that when the ground shook, messages arose from the deep." None of you would try to explain that message by the tides or the water or the wind. You would know that the only plausible explanation for those markings is an intelligent mind.

paragraphs.heading: An author of life
paragraphs.edited: We find more information in DNA than in anything humans can invent. That's why the best explanation for the DNA we see in nature, and in the human body in particular, is that it comes from an intelligent designer, an author of life.
